questions.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with a 3-month history of intermittent abdominal pain, diarrhea and weight loss. She reports that her stools are sometimes bloody. She also mentions occasional mouth ulcers and a recent episode of joint pain in her knees. Physical examination reveals mild tenderness in the right lower quadrant and oral aphthous ulcers. Laboratory tests show anemia and elevated inflammatory markers. Colonoscopy reveals patchy, transmural inflammation with skip lesions and areas of cobblestone appearance. Biopsy confirms granulomatous inflammation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
e:
Intermittent abdominal pain, diarrhoea, weight loss, oral aphthous ulcers, arthralgia, skip lesions, cobblestoning and granulomas on biopsy = Crohn's disease. Extra-intestinal features (aphthous ulcers, arthritis) are common.
Crohn's extra-intestinal manifestations: aphthae, arthritis, erythema nodosum, uveitis.

questions.q: A 32-year-old female presents to the outpatient clinic with complaints of intermittent abdominal pain, diarrhea and weight loss over the past six months. Colonoscopy shows colonic and terminal ileum longitudinal ulcers with cobblestone appearance. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?
e:
The image shows longitudinal ulcers and cobblestoning in the colon and terminal ileum in a young woman with chronic pain, diarrhoea and weight loss: Crohn's disease. IBS has no ulcers, and infective gastroenteritis is acute.
Terminal ileum + cobblestone = Crohn's.

questions.q: Colonoscopy shows deep colonic ulcers with inflamed surrounding mucosa. These lesions can present by:
e:
Deep ulcers with inflamed surrounding mucosa on colonoscopy (image) may present with bleeding per rectum, diarrhoea and abdominal pain, so all of the above.
Colonic ulceration: bleeding + diarrhoea + pain; confirm with biopsy.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with bloody diarrhea, abdominal cramping and urgency for the past 2 weeks. She reports passing mixed stool with blood and mucus. She has no fever or weight loss. She has a history of multiple previous similar episodes. On examination, she appears pale and has mild tenderness in the lower abdomen. What is a common hematological complication associated with her condition that explains her pallor?
o: Iron deficiency anemia due to chronic blood loss
Vitamin B12 deficiency due to malabsorption
e:
Recurrent bloody diarrhoea with mucus (ulcerative colitis picture) causes chronic blood loss, so iron deficiency anaemia is the common haematological complication. B12 deficiency occurs with terminal ileal Crohn's, and haemolysis is a rare autoimmune complication.
IBD anaemia: iron deficiency (blood loss) ± chronic disease ± B12/folate deficiency.

questions.q: Colonoscopy shows diffuse ulceration involving the rectum and extending to the sigmoid colon. The next investigation is:
e:
The image shows diffuse rectosigmoid ulceration; the next investigation is a mucosal biopsy (at colonoscopy) to confirm the diagnosis (UC vs Crohn's vs infection) and exclude malignancy. CT, CBC and stool analysis are supportive but not the definitive next step.
Colonoscopy + biopsies is the gold standard for IBD diagnosis.

questions.q: Colonoscopy shows diffuse ulceration involving the rectum and extending to the sigmoid colon with skip areas and cobblestone appearance. The next investigation is:
e:
The image shows rectosigmoid ulceration with skip areas and a cobblestone appearance, the pattern of Crohn's disease. The next step is biopsy, which confirms the diagnosis (transmural inflammation, granulomas) and excludes TB or cancer. Tumour markers, CBC and stool analysis do not give a diagnosis.
Cobblestoning + skip lesions → biopsy to prove Crohn's.

questions.q: Which of the following is a marker of the excretory function of the liver?
e: Conjugated (direct) bilirubin reflects the excretory function of the liver — its secretion into bile; raised bilirubin in cirrhosis is due to impaired hepatocyte excretory function. Albumin and total protein reflect synthetic function; ALP is a cholestatic enzyme. Liver function: excretory (bilirubin), synthetic (albumin, PT), enzymes (ALT/AST/ALP/GGT).

questions.q: Which of the following imaging techniques is considered the best first-line investigation for evaluating liver pathology?
e:
Abdominal ultrasound is the best first-line imaging for liver disease: cheap, safe, non-invasive, and it detects focal lesions, bile duct dilatation, cirrhosis and ascites. CT and MRI are second-line; plain X-ray gives little information.
Ultrasound first for liver and biliary problems.

questions.q: The investigation to start with to reach the diagnosis is:
e:
The photo shows icteric (yellow) sclerae. The investigation to start with in jaundice is abdominal ultrasound, to detect biliary dilatation, stones, masses and signs of cirrhosis. CT, biopsy and ERCP are done afterwards as indicated.
Jaundice: history, LFTs, then ultrasound to separate obstructive from non-obstructive.

questions.q: The investigation to start with to reach the diagnosis is:
e:
The photo shows icteric (yellow) sclerae. The investigation to start with in a jaundiced patient is abdominal ultrasound, which shows bile duct dilatation, stones, masses and the state of the liver. CT, liver biopsy and tumour markers are not first-line.
Jaundice: history, LFTs, then ultrasound first.

questions.q: The investigation to start with to reach the diagnosis is:
e:
The image shows jaundice (yellow sclerae). Abdominal ultrasound is the investigation to start with. MRI and biopsy come later if needed, and transaminases show liver cell injury but do not locate the cause.
Always image the biliary tree first with ultrasound.

questions.q: The investigation to start with to reach the diagnosis is:
e:
The image shows jaundiced eyes. Abdominal ultrasound is the investigation to start with; MRI and ERCP are used later when needed, and biopsy is not first-line.
Dilated bile ducts on ultrasound point to obstructive jaundice.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with yellowing of her skin and sclera. On physical examination, you note the following findings: pallor, mild hepatomegaly and dark urine. The patient reports no abdominal pain or fever. What is the next most important initial investigation in a case of jaundice?
e:
The image shows jaundiced eyes. In a patient with pallor, mild hepatomegaly and dark urine, the next most important initial investigation is abdominal ultrasound to look for biliary obstruction and liver changes. Upper endoscopy, ERCP and liver biopsy come later.
Dilated bile ducts on ultrasound → obstructive jaundice.

questions.q: A predominantly direct (conjugated) hyperbilirubinemia is present in all of the following causes of jaundice, except:
e:
Obstruction (bile duct obstruction), drug-induced injury and primary biliary cirrhosis cause predominantly conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia. Haemolysis increases unconjugated bilirubin, so it is the exception.
Haemolysis: unconjugated, no bilirubin in urine (acholuric jaundice).

questions.q: A 52-year-old woman with a history of hepatitis B presents with yellowing of her skin and sclera for two weeks. She also reports dark urine and pale stools. On examination, she has jaundice, hepatomegaly and tenderness in the right upper quadrant. Laboratory tests show elevated bilirubin (both direct and indirect) and elevated liver enzymes. What is the most probable cause of her jaundice?
o: Liver cell injury causing hepatocellular jaundice
e:
Jaundice with both direct and indirect bilirubin elevation, raised liver enzymes, hepatomegaly and tenderness in a patient with hepatitis B is hepatocellular jaundice (liver cell injury). The image shows scleral icterus. Haemolysis and neonatal jaundice are unconjugated, and pure obstruction would have a cholestatic pattern.
Hepatocellular jaundice: mixed hyperbilirubinaemia with high ALT/AST.

questions.q: A 45-year-old man presents with fatigue and this sign. Laboratory tests reveal elevated serum bilirubin, predominantly direct (conjugated), along with elevated liver enzymes (ALT and AST). Ultrasound shows hepatomegaly without biliary obstruction. Which of the following best describes the pathophysiology of his jaundice?
o: Obstruction of the common bile duct leading to accumulation of conjugated bilirubin
Increased production of bilirubin due to hemolysis
Impaired conjugation and excretion of bilirubin by the hepatocytes
Infiltration of the liver by metastatic tumor causing ductal compression
e:
The image shows icteric sclerae. Predominantly direct bilirubin, raised ALT/AST and hepatomegaly without biliary obstruction on ultrasound indicates hepatocellular jaundice: impaired conjugation and excretion by damaged hepatocytes.
No ductal dilatation on ultrasound → intrahepatic (hepatocellular) cause.

questions.q: A 55-year-old man presents with this finding, which has developed gradually over the past two weeks. He also reports fatigue, dark urine and occasional nausea. On physical examination, no hepatomegaly or abdominal tenderness is observed. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism for this finding?
o: Increased unconjugated bilirubin due to hemolysis
Increased conjugated bilirubin due to biliary obstruction
Decreased bilirubin production from liver failure
Increased serum bilirubin due to excessive hemolysis and impaired conjugation
Decreased bilirubin excretion due to renal failure
e:
The image shows jaundice with dark urine and a gradual onset without hepatomegaly; the keyed mechanism is obstruction to bile flow, increasing conjugated bilirubin (dark urine = bilirubinuria). Haemolysis gives unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, and renal failure does not cause jaundice.
Dark urine means conjugated bilirubin (water soluble) is raised.

questions.q: A 35-year-old female presents with yellowing of the skin and sclera for the past week. She reports dark urine and pale stools. She has a history of recurrent colicky right hypochondrial pain after fatty meals. On examination, she appears icteric. Laboratory tests show: total bilirubin 6.0 mg/dL (direct bilirubin 4.5 mg/dL); elevated ALT, AST and alkaline phosphatase; viral hepatitis panel negative. Abdominal ultrasound: calculous gallbladder, dilated intrahepatic biliary radicles and dilated CBD. What is the most likely type of jaundice in this patient, and the underlying mechanism?
o: Hemolytic jaundice; increased unconjugated bilirubin due to hemolysis
Obstructive jaundice; increased conjugated bilirubin due to biliary obstruction
Hepatocellular jaundice; mixed unconjugated and conjugated bilirubin due to hepatocyte injury
Neonatal jaundice; physiological process in newborns
e:
Pale stools, dark urine, colicky pain after fatty meals, direct bilirubin 4.5 of 6.0 mg/dL, high ALP and a calculous gallbladder with dilated ducts = obstructive jaundice from biliary obstruction (image: icteric sclerae).
Obstructive jaundice: pale stools, dark urine, itching, high ALP/GGT.

questions.q: A 50-year-old male presents to the emergency department with this finding, dark urine and pale stools for the last week. He reports colicky right hypochondrial pain with nausea. What is the most likely cause in this patient?
e:
Jaundice (image) with dark urine, pale stools and colicky right hypochondrial pain is choledocholithiasis (common bile duct stone). Alcoholic hepatocellular damage and hepatitis A do not cause pale stools with biliary colic, and haemolysis has no pain.
Charcot's triad (pain, fever, jaundice) suggests ascending cholangitis.

questions.q: A 45-year-old man presents with yellowing of his skin and eyes for the past week. He reports dark urine and pale stools. He also mentions mild abdominal discomfort in the right upper quadrant. On examination, his sclerae are icteric, and there is tenderness in the right upper abdomen. Liver function tests reveal elevated conjugated bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase. What is the most likely cause of his jaundice?
e:
Jaundice with dark urine, pale stools, right upper quadrant discomfort and raised conjugated bilirubin and ALP indicates biliary obstruction. Haemolysis and Gilbert's syndrome cause unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia; viral hepatitis and cirrhosis give a hepatocellular pattern.
High ALP + high direct bilirubin = cholestasis/obstruction.

questions.q: A 52-year-old man presents with fatigue, abdominal swelling and occasional episodes of easy bruising. He has a history of alcohol use for over 20 years. Physical examination reveals jaundice, hepatomegaly, ascites and spider angiomata on his chest. Laboratory tests show elevated liver enzymes, low albumin and prolonged prothrombin time. An abdominal ultrasound demonstrates a shrunken, nodular liver with irregular borders, splenomegaly and evidence of ascites. What is the most likely diagnosis based on the ultrasound findings?
e:
The ultrasound image shows a shrunken, nodular liver with irregular borders, splenomegaly and ascites in a long-term alcohol user: liver cirrhosis. HCC would be a focal lesion, fatty liver is bright and enlarged, and acute hepatitis/abscess do not give a nodular small liver.
Cirrhosis on ultrasound: small nodular liver, coarse echotexture, splenomegaly, ascites.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman with a history of alcohol use presents with abdominal distension, jaundice and fatigue. An abdominal ultrasound is performed to evaluate her liver. The ultrasound reveals a small, nodular liver with surface irregularities, splenomegaly and evidence of ascites. Which of the following ultrasound findings is most characteristic of liver cirrhosis?
o: Small, nodular liver with surface irregularities and coarse echotexture
Large, homogenous liver with increased vascularity
Multiple cysts throughout the liver parenchyma
e:
The image shows a cirrhotic liver. The characteristic ultrasound appearance is a small, nodular liver with surface irregularity and coarse echotexture; enlarged smooth, homogeneous or cystic livers are other conditions.
Look at the liver edge: nodular = cirrhosis.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with progressive abdominal distension and fatigue. An abdominal ultrasound is performed, revealing a shrunken, nodular liver with irregular margins, increased echogenicity and the presence of moderate free fluid in the abdominal cavity. No focal hepatic lesions are identified. Laboratory tests show elevated liver enzymes, low serum albumin and an increased INR. Which of the following ultrasound findings most likely explains her clinical presentation?
o: Cirrhotic liver with portal hypertension and ascites
e:
The ultrasound shows a cirrhotic liver with free abdominal fluid; with raised enzymes, low albumin and high INR this is cirrhosis with portal hypertension and ascites. A tumour with vascular invasion would show a focal mass, fatty liver is enlarged and bright, and acute hepatitis is not shrunken.
Low albumin + prolonged INR + ascites = decompensation (impaired synthetic function).

questions.q: A 45-year-old male with chronic hepatitis C presents with abdominal distension and leg swelling. Which of the following findings indicates decompensated liver disease?
e:
Ascites is a sign of decompensated liver disease (portal hypertension and hypoalbuminaemia), as are jaundice, encephalopathy and variceal bleeding. Hepatomegaly and elevated ALT show liver disease but not decompensation, and thrombocytosis is not seen (thrombocytopenia is).
Decompensation = ascites, jaundice, encephalopathy, variceal bleeding.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a complication of hepatic cirrhosis?
e:
Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis and hepatocellular carcinoma are complications of cirrhosis. Thrombocytosis is not; cirrhosis causes thrombocytopenia due to hypersplenism and low thrombopoietin.
Platelets fall early in cirrhosis; a low platelet count suggests portal hypertension.

questions.q: A 48-year-old man presents with fatigue, weakness and swelling in his legs. He has a history of hepatitis B infection. On examination, his liver is enlarged, and he has spider angiomata on his face. Blood tests show elevated bilirubin and low serum albumin. Which complication is he most at risk for due to his cirrhosis?
e: In chronic hepatitis B with cirrhosis, he is most at risk of liver cancer (hepatocellular carcinoma), which can occur in HBV even without cirrhosis; spider angiomata and an enlarged liver support chronic liver disease. Kidney failure (hepatorenal syndrome) is also a complication of cirrhosis. Heart failure and pneumonia are not specific. Cirrhosis + HBV/HCV: ultrasound ± AFP every 6 months for HCC surveillance.

questions.q: Causes of ascites include all of the following except:
e:
Nephrotic syndrome (low albumin), right heart failure (congestion) and cirrhosis cause ascites. Anaemia does not, so it is the exception.
Ascites causes: cirrhosis, heart failure, nephrotic syndrome, malignancy, TB, Budd-Chiari.

questions.q: Causes of ascites include all of the following except:
e:
Nephrotic syndrome, right heart failure and malignancy are causes of ascites; acute diarrhoea causes dehydration, not ascites, so it is the exception.
Think transudate (cirrhosis, HF, nephrotic) vs exudate (TB, malignancy).

questions.q: Causes of ascites include all of the following except:
e:
Nephrotic syndrome, portal hypertension and tuberculosis (peritoneal TB) cause ascites. HIV infection itself is not a direct cause of ascites, so it is the exception.
TB peritonitis: exudative ascites with high lymphocytes and high ADA.

questions.q: The most common cause of ascites is:
e:
Liver cirrhosis is by far the most common cause of ascites (portal hypertension plus hypoalbuminaemia). Nephrotic syndrome, right heart failure and anaemia are less common or not causes.
Commonest cause of ascites worldwide: cirrhosis (HBV/HCV in Egypt).

questions.q: The most common cause of ascites is:
e:
Liver cirrhosis is by far the most common cause of ascites. Nephrotic syndrome, Meigs' syndrome (ovarian fibroma with ascites and pleural effusion) and ovarian cancer are much less common causes.
Meigs' syndrome: ovarian fibroma + ascites + right pleural effusion.

questions.q: A 60-year-old male presents to the outpatient clinic with complaints of increasing abdominal distension. He has a history of chronic hepatitis C and alcohol use disorder. On physical examination he showed this finding. What is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's ascites?
o: Cirrhosis secondary to chronic liver disease
e:
The image shows a distended abdomen. In a patient with chronic hepatitis C and alcohol use disorder, the most likely cause of ascites is cirrhosis secondary to chronic liver disease. Heart failure, nephrotic syndrome and peritoneal carcinomatosis are less likely.
Chronic hepatitis + alcohol → cirrhosis → ascites.

questions.q: A 60-year-old woman presents with abdominal distension, discomfort and weight gain over the past few weeks. She has a history of chronic alcohol use. On examination, her abdomen is distended with shifting dullness. Laboratory tests show: serum albumin 2.8 g/dL; ascitic fluid analysis with a serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) of 1.8 g/dL; elevated liver enzymes and bilirubin. What is the most likely cause of her ascites?
e:
A serum-ascites albumin gradient of 1.8 g/dL (≥ 1.1) indicates portal hypertension; with chronic alcohol use, low albumin and raised liver enzymes this is cirrhosis. Malignant peritoneal disease and TB have a low SAAG; nephrotic syndrome also has a low SAAG; CHF has high SAAG but a high ascitic protein.
SAAG ≥ 1.1 g/dL = portal hypertension; < 1.1 = peritoneal causes.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man with a history of alcohol use presents with abdominal distension, discomfort and a weight gain of 4 kg over the past month. On examination, his abdomen is distended with shifting dullness. There is no jaundice or peripheral edema. Laboratory tests reveal serum albumin of 2.8 g/dL, elevated liver enzymes and a serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) of 2.2 g/dL. Paracentesis yields straw-colored fluid with a high SAAG and a total protein level of 1.5 g/dL. What is the most likely cause of this patient's ascites?
e:
The image shows a distended abdomen. SAAG 2.2 g/dL (high) with low ascitic protein (1.5 g/dL, below 2.5) and a background of alcohol use points to cirrhosis. Heart failure gives high SAAG but high ascitic protein; carcinomatosis gives a low SAAG.
High SAAG + low protein → cirrhosis; high SAAG + high protein → cardiac or Budd-Chiari.

questions.q: Which statement regarding spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) is incorrect?
o: Diagnosis is confirmed by paracentesis with WBCs ≥ 250 cells/mm³, mainly polymorphonuclear leucocytes
The most common bacteria are Gram positive
e:
In spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, diagnosis is by paracentesis with ≥ 250 neutrophils/mm³, cultures are often negative, and cefotaxime is a standard treatment. The most common bacteria are Gram-negative (E. coli, Klebsiella), not Gram-positive, so statement C is incorrect.
SBP: ascitic PMN ≥ 250/mm³ → treat with IV cefotaxime + albumin; secondary prophylaxis with norfloxacin.

questions.q: A 48-year-old man presents with complaints of abdominal distension, easy bruising and episodes of vomiting blood. He reports a history of hepatitis B infection. On examination, he has distended abdominal veins (caput medusae), splenomegaly and signs of ascites. Laboratory tests show elevated liver enzymes and low serum albumin. What is the most likely pathophysiological mechanism responsible for his clinical findings?
o: Obstruction of the hepatic veins leading to Budd-Chiari syndrome
Increased resistance to portal blood flow due to cirrhosis
Obstruction of the hepatic artery causing ischemia
Increased portal vein flow due to arteriovenous fistula
Congenital absence of the portal vein
e:
Caput medusae, splenomegaly, ascites and haematemesis in cirrhosis result from portal hypertension, caused by increased resistance to portal blood flow within the cirrhotic liver. Budd-Chiari (hepatic vein block), hepatic artery obstruction, AV fistula and congenital portal vein absence are rarer.
Portal hypertension = increased resistance (cirrhosis) ± increased flow.

questions.q: Upper endoscopy showing bluish cords protruding into the lumen of the esophagus. The diagnosis of these lesions can be:
e:
The endoscopy image shows bluish tortuous cords protruding into the oesophageal lumen: oesophageal varices. A Mallory-Weiss tear is a mucosal laceration, a stricture is a narrowing and GERD shows inflamed mucosa.
Oesophageal varices: blue, tortuous columns in the lower oesophagus; risk grows with size and red spots.

questions.q: A 50-year-old patient presents to the emergency department with vomiting of bright red blood. He has no prior medical history and is not on anticoagulant medications. Based on the finding in the upper endoscopy study (bluish cords protruding into the lumen of the esophagus), which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
e:
Hematemesis with bluish cords protruding into the lumen on endoscopy is oesophageal variceal bleeding. Gastric ulcer, Mallory-Weiss tear, gastritis and carcinoma have different endoscopic appearances.
Variceal bleeding is life-threatening: resuscitate, vasoactive drug, antibiotics, endoscopic band ligation.

questions.q: A 58-year-old male presents to the emergency department with complaints of vomiting blood and black tarry stools. On examination, he appears pale. His vital signs show a blood pressure of 90/60 mmHg, heart rate of 115 bpm and a temperature of 98.6 °F. Upper endoscopy shows bluish cords protruding into the lumen of the esophagus. What is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's symptoms?
o: Esophageal varices due to portal hypertension
e:
The image shows bluish oesophageal varices. With hematemesis, melaena, hypotension and tachycardia, the cause is oesophageal varices due to portal hypertension (usually cirrhosis). Peptic ulcer, gastric cancer and oesophagitis do not show varices.
Varices need portal hypertension (portal pressure gradient > 10 mmHg).

questions.q: A 50-year-old man with a history of chronic alcohol abuse and hepatitis B infection presents to the emergency department with vomiting of large amounts of bright red blood. He reports feeling dizzy and weak. On examination, he appears pale and hypotensive. Jugular venous distension is noted, along with distended abdominal veins (caput medusae). The abdomen is tender in the epigastric region. Laboratory tests reveal anemia and elevated liver enzymes. What is the most probable cause of his hematemesis?
o: Esophageal varices secondary to portal hypertension
e:
Alcohol, hepatitis B, caput medusae, pallor and hypotension with massive bright red hematemesis indicate bleeding oesophageal varices secondary to portal hypertension. Peptic ulcer, Mallory-Weiss tear, carcinoma and polyp are less likely.
Caput medusae + haematemesis = think portal hypertension.

questions.q: Upper endoscopy in a patient presenting with hematemesis showed dilated tortuous veins with cherry-red spots. The cause of this finding is:
e:
The image shows dilated tortuous veins with cherry-red spots at upper endoscopy: oesophageal varices. The most likely cause is liver cirrhosis (portal hypertension). Cherry-red spots mark a high risk of bleeding.
Cherry-red spots / red wale marks → high-risk varices.

questions.q: Upper endoscopy in a patient known to have liver cirrhosis, presenting with hematemesis, described dilated tortuous veins with cherry-red spots. The cause of this finding is:
e:
Dilated tortuous oesophageal veins with cherry-red spots (image) in a patient with cirrhosis mean oesophageal varices from portal hypertension; the keyed cause is portal vein thrombosis (pre-hepatic portal obstruction). Oesophagitis, gastritis and peptic ulcer do not produce varices. Note: this is the original bank's answer. Strictly, the cause of the varices is portal hypertension (portal vein thrombosis is one cause of it).
Portal vein thrombosis is the commonest pre-hepatic cause of portal hypertension.

questions.q: A 60-year-old male patient, known HCV liver cirrhosis, presents with hematemesis and melena. BP = 90/60, pulse = 110/min, Hb = 6.5 g/dL. Management includes:
e: BP 90/60, pulse 110/min and Hb 6.5 g/dL signal haemorrhagic shock from variceal bleeding. Management includes resuscitation, blood transfusion and upper endoscopy (band ligation), so all of the above. Transfuse cautiously in variceal bleeding (target Hb 7 g/dL); over-transfusion raises portal pressure.

questions.q: A 50-year-old male patient presenting with hematemesis; upper endoscopy showed these lesions (bluish cords protruding into the lumen of the esophagus). Which laboratory investigation would you recommend as the initial investigation to assess the patient?
e:
The image shows oesophageal varices in a patient with hematemesis; the initial laboratory investigation is a complete blood picture to assess blood loss (Hb). Gastrin, H. pylori serology and ABG are not first-line tests here.
Initial labs in GI bleeding: CBC, coagulation profile, liver and kidney function, cross-match.

questions.q: A 50-year-old male patient presents with hematemesis. Upper endoscopy showed these lesions (bluish cords protruding into the lumen of the esophagus). The next step is:
e:
The image shows oesophageal varices. For bleeding varices at endoscopy, endoscopic variceal band ligation is the treatment of choice (with a vasoactive drug and antibiotics). Conservative management alone is inadequate, biopsy is dangerous and argon plasma coagulation is for vascular ectasia such as GAVE.
Acute variceal bleeding: terlipressin/octreotide + antibiotics + band ligation.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man with cirrhosis undergoes endoscopy for screening and is found to have this finding (upper endoscopy showing bluish cords protruding into the lumen of the esophagus). He has no history of variceal bleeding. His Child-Pugh score is A. What is the recommended management at this stage?
o: Start non-selective beta-blockers (e.g., propranolol) for primary prophylaxis
e:
In a Child-Pugh A cirrhotic patient with varices that have never bled, primary prophylaxis with non-selective beta-blockers (propranolol/carvedilol) is recommended (image shows the varices). Surveillance alone is not enough for varices, and immediate banding is for bleeding or beta-blocker intolerance/contraindication.
Primary prophylaxis: non-selective β-blocker or band ligation; secondary prophylaxis after a bleed: both.

questions.q: A 30-year-old man presents with fatigue, nausea, right upper quadrant abdominal pain and jaundice that developed over the past week. He reports recent travel to a region with poor sanitation. Laboratory tests show elevated liver enzymes and positive IgM anti-HAV antibodies. There is no history of alcohol use or IV drug use. Which of the following is the most characteristic feature of hepatitis A infection?
o: It causes chronic hepatitis in most cases.
It is transmitted primarily through contaminated water and food.
It is associated with a high risk of hepatocellular carcinoma.
It typically presents with a prolonged, relapsing course.
It is transmitted via blood transfusion in most cases.
e:
Hepatitis A is spread by the faecal-oral route through contaminated water and food; the illness is self-limiting and never becomes chronic. It does not cause chronic hepatitis, HCC or blood-borne spread.
IgM anti-HAV = acute infection; vaccine available.

questions.q: Which statement is false regarding acute hepatitis A?
o: Usually mild to moderate in severity and worse in adults than in children
e:
Hepatitis A is usually mild-moderate, worse in adults than children, spreads by the faeco-oral route and can be severe in pregnancy. Chronic hepatitis never occurs with HAV, so the false statement is B.
HAV and HEV do not become chronic (HEV can in immunosuppressed patients).

questions.q: Which of the following is not a cause of acute hepatitis?
e:
Autoimmune hepatitis, CMV and mushroom (Amanita) poisoning can present as acute hepatitis. Bilharziasis (schistosomiasis) causes chronic periportal fibrosis, not acute hepatitis, so it is the exception.
Schistosomiasis: periportal (pipe-stem) fibrosis with preserved liver function.

questions.q: A 30-year-old man from an area with poor sanitation presents with sudden onset of jaundice, dark urine, fatigue and nausea. He reports recent consumption of contaminated water while traveling. Physical examination reveals scleral icterus and hepatomegaly. Laboratory tests show elevated serum bilirubin (predominantly direct), raised ALT and AST levels, and negative markers for hepatitis B and C. What is the most likely diagnosis, and what is the characteristic histological feature of this disease?
o: Hepatitis B; ground-glass hepatocytes with intranuclear inclusions
Hepatitis C; lymphoid aggregates and piecemeal necrosis
Hepatitis A; ballooning degeneration of hepatocytes and Councilman bodies
Autoimmune hepatitis; interface hepatitis with plasma cell infiltrates
e: Contaminated water in a young man, acute jaundice and negative HBV/HCV markers = hepatitis A. Acute viral hepatitis shows ballooning degeneration of hepatocytes with Councilman (acidophilic) bodies. Ground-glass cells are HBV, piecemeal necrosis/lymphoid aggregates are HCV, and plasma cell interface hepatitis is autoimmune. Ground-glass hepatocytes = chronic HBV; Councilman bodies = apoptotic hepatocytes in acute viral hepatitis.

questions.q: A 35-year-old male presents to the outpatient clinic with fatigue, nausea and mild abdominal discomfort. He reports no significant medical history and does not take any medications. He mentions he has had multiple sexual partners in the past year and has not received the hepatitis B vaccine. On examination, he has mild jaundice and tenderness in the right upper quadrant. Laboratory tests reveal markedly elevated liver enzymes (AST and ALT) and positive hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) and hepatitis B core IgM antibody (HBcIgM). What is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?
e:
Positive HBsAg with IgM anti-HBc (core IgM) and markedly high ALT/AST = acute hepatitis B. Chronic HBV has IgG anti-HBc and persistent HBsAg for > 6 months; HAV and HCV have different serology.
IgM anti-HBc = acute (or window period if HBsAg negative).

questions.q: A 30-year-old healthcare worker presents for routine screening. She reports no symptoms but has a history of multiple sexual partners. Blood tests show positive hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) and hepatitis B e antigen (HBeAg). Liver function tests are normal. Which of the following statements is true regarding hepatitis B infection?
o: HBsAg positivity indicates immunity to HBV
HBeAg positivity suggests active viral replication and high infectivity
The presence of anti-HBs antibodies indicates current infection
HBV is transmitted primarily through the fecal-oral route
There is no available vaccine for HBV
e:
HBeAg positivity reflects active viral replication and high infectivity. HBsAg means infection, not immunity (immunity = anti-HBs); HBV spreads by blood, sex and vertical transmission, not faeco-orally; a vaccine exists.
HBsAg + HBeAg + high DNA = highly infectious.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman from an endemic area presents with fatigue, jaundice and right upper quadrant discomfort. Laboratory tests show elevated ALT and AST, with positive HBsAg and HBeAg. She reports no recent alcohol intake or drug use. What is the primary cause of her liver enzyme elevation, and what is the likely pathology seen histologically?
o: Alcoholic hepatitis; fatty change and ballooning degeneration
Viral hepatitis B; interface hepatitis with lymphocytic infiltration and hepatocyte necrosis
Autoimmune hepatitis; plasma cell infiltration with rosettes
Cirrhosis; bridging fibrosis with regenerative nodules
e: HBsAg and HBeAg positivity in a patient with jaundice and raised enzymes indicates viral hepatitis B with interface hepatitis, lymphocytic infiltration and hepatocyte necrosis. Alcohol and autoimmune hepatitis are excluded by history and serology, and cirrhosis is not implied. HBV hepatitis histology: lymphocytic infiltrate and hepatocyte necrosis; chronic: ground-glass cells.

questions.q: A 35-year-old man from an endemic area presents with fatigue, weakness and occasional right upper quadrant discomfort. He reports a history of unprotected sex and intravenous drug use in his youth. Physical examination reveals mild hepatomegaly. Laboratory tests show elevated ALT, positive HBsAg and anti-HBc antibodies. HBV DNA levels are high. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
e:
HBsAg, anti-HBc, high HBV DNA and raised ALT mean chronic active HBV; start antiviral therapy (tenofovir/entecavir). Observation is for inactive carriers, vaccination is not treatment, and biopsy is not mandatory.
Treat HBV when ALT is raised with high DNA, or fibrosis is present.

questions.q: A 32-year-old man presents with fatigue, right upper quadrant discomfort and occasional jaundice. He reports having multiple sexual partners in the past. On examination, he has mild hepatomegaly but no ascites or encephalopathy. Laboratory tests reveal elevated ALT and AST levels, positive hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), positive hepatitis B e antigen (HBeAg) and high levels of hepatitis B DNA. A liver biopsy shows chronic hepatitis with mild fibrosis. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
e:
HBeAg-positive chronic hepatitis B with high DNA, raised transaminases and fibrosis on biopsy needs antiviral therapy with tenofovir. Steroids can flare HBV, transplantation is for decompensation, and the vaccine does not treat established infection.
First-line HBV nucleos(t)ides: tenofovir or entecavir (high barrier to resistance).

questions.q: A 50-year-old man with a history of intravenous drug use presents with fatigue, right upper quadrant discomfort and jaundice. Liver function tests show elevated ALT and AST. Serologic testing reveals positive anti-HCV antibodies and detectable HCV RNA. Which of the following is the primary mode of transmission for his condition?
o: Vertical transmission from mother to child
Blood-to-blood contact, such as sharing needles
e:
Hepatitis C is mainly transmitted by blood-to-blood contact (sharing needles, transfusion, unsafe injections). Sexual and vertical spread are less efficient, and food/water or respiratory spread does not occur.
HCV is the commonest bloodborne hepatitis; IV drug use is the main risk.

questions.q: A 50-year-old man with a history of intravenous drug use presents for evaluation. He reports fatigue and occasional right upper quadrant discomfort. Blood tests reveal elevated liver enzymes. Serologic testing shows positive anti-HCV antibodies, and HCV RNA is detectable, confirming active infection. He denies jaundice or significant alcohol use. What is the primary mode of transmission for hepatitis C virus (HCV)?
e:
HCV spreads by parenteral exposure (blood-to-blood contact). Faecal-oral and droplet routes are not involved, and sexual and vertical transmission are minor.
HCV: anti-HCV positive, then HCV RNA (PCR) confirms active infection.

questions.q: A 50-year-old woman with a history of intravenous drug use presents with fatigue and mild right upper quadrant discomfort. She reports recent unintentional weight loss. Laboratory tests show elevated ALT and AST. HCV antibody test is positive; HCV RNA is detectable at high levels. What is the most suitable management approach?
o: No treatment, as HCV resolves spontaneously
e:
Active HCV infection (anti-HCV positive, high RNA) should be treated with direct-acting antivirals, which cure over 95%. Watchful waiting is inappropriate, transplantation is for decompensation, and HCV rarely resolves spontaneously in a symptomatic patient with high RNA.
DAAs (e.g. sofosbuvir-based) for 8–12 weeks: SVR > 95%.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with fatigue and intermittent right upper quadrant discomfort. She reports a history of intravenous drug use in her early 20s but has been abstinent for several years. She denies alcohol use. On examination, she appears well but has mild hepatomegaly. Laboratory tests reveal elevated ALT and AST levels. Serology shows positive anti- HCV antibodies, and subsequent PCR testing confirms active hepatitis C infection with a viral load of 2 million IU/mL. Liver biopsy indicates chronic hepatitis with mild fibrosis. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Start antiviral therapy with direct-acting antivirals (DAAs)
e:
Active HCV infection with a high viral load, even with mild fibrosis, is treated with direct-acting antivirals. Steroids, observation only and transplant are inappropriate, and there is no vaccine for hepatitis C.
There is no HCV vaccine; treat everyone with detectable RNA.

questions.q: A 55-year-old man with a history of intravenous drug use presents for routine screening. He reports no current symptoms but mentions fatigue. Liver function tests show mildly elevated ALT and AST. HCV antibody test is positive, and subsequent PCR confirms active viral replication. Which is the most common mode of transmission for hepatitis C virus?
o: Vertical transmission from mother to child
Blood-to-blood contact, such as sharing needles
e: HCV is mainly transmitted by blood-to-blood contact — sharing needles in intravenous drug use, transfusion and unsafe injections — which fits this asymptomatic patient found on routine screening with positive anti-HCV and PCR. Sexual and vertical spread are less efficient; contaminated food and water is the faecal-oral route of HAV and HEV, and respiratory droplets do not transmit HCV.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman presents with sudden onset of severe right upper quadrant abdominal pain, hepatomegaly, ascites and jaundice. She has a history of oral contraceptive use. Doppler ultrasound of the liver shows absent or reversed flow in the hepatic veins. Which of the following is the most characteristic finding in Budd-Chiari syndrome?
o: Obstruction of the hepatic veins leading to congestion and hepatomegaly
Obstruction of the portal vein causing portal hypertension
Obstruction of the inferior vena cava below the hepatic veins
Multiple cystic lesions in the liver
e:
The image shows dilated abdominal wall veins in a woman with sudden RUQ pain, hepatomegaly, ascites, jaundice, oral contraceptive use and absent/reversed hepatic vein flow: Budd-Chiari syndrome. It is characterised by obstruction of the hepatic veins leading to hepatic congestion and hepatomegaly.
Budd-Chiari: hepatic vein/IVC outflow obstruction; look for prothrombotic states (OCP, polycythaemia, PNH).

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with sudden onset of severe right upper quadrant abdominal pain; inspection of the abdomen showed this finding. She has a history of oral contraceptive use. Doppler ultrasound reveals absence of flow in the hepatic veins. Laboratory tests show elevated liver enzymes and mild coagulopathy. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
e:
The image shows prominent dilated veins on the abdominal wall. Sudden RUQ pain, oral contraceptive use, absent hepatic vein flow on Doppler and coagulopathy indicate Budd-Chiari syndrome. Cirrhosis would be chronic, and heart failure does not cause absent hepatic vein flow.
Absent hepatic vein flow on Doppler = Budd-Chiari.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with a 2-week history of abdominal pain, hepatomegaly and ascites. She reports feeling fatigued and has noticed swelling in her legs. She has no significant past medical history but mentions recent use of oral contraceptives. Physical examination reveals tender hepatomegaly, ascites and lower limb edema. Liver function tests show elevated bilirubin and mildly increased transaminases. Doppler ultrasound of the abdomen shows absence of flow in the hepatic veins. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Cirrhosis secondary to chronic hepatitis B
Congestive heart failure with hepatic congestion
e:
Tender hepatomegaly, ascites, leg oedema, raised bilirubin and absent hepatic vein flow in a woman taking oral contraceptives indicate Budd-Chiari syndrome. Cirrhosis would not present acutely, and congestive heart failure/metastases do not abolish hepatic vein flow.
OCP is a recognised thrombotic risk factor for Budd-Chiari.

questions.q: A 42-year-old female presents to the emergency department with a 2-week history of worsening abdominal pain, along with increasing fatigue and leg swelling. She reports recent weight gain. On examination, there is marked tenderness in the right upper quadrant, and the liver is palpably enlarged. There is also notable ascites and bilateral lower extremity edema, and this clinical finding. What is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?
e: The image shows dilated abdominal wall veins with marked RUQ tenderness, hepatomegaly, ascites and bilateral leg oedema over 2 weeks: Budd-Chiari syndrome (hepatic vein/IVC outflow obstruction) fits best. Cirrhosis is chronic, a hepatic adenoma would not cause oedema and ascites, and acute portal vein thrombosis presents with severe abdominal pain but minimal liver-test changes and without this outflow-obstruction picture. Tender hepatomegaly + ascites + leg oedema = Budd-Chiari.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man with a history of chronic hepatitis B presents with weight loss, right upper quadrant pain and jaundice. Ultrasound reveals a large liver mass with irregular borders. Serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) levels are elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
e:
A large irregular liver mass with raised AFP in a patient with chronic hepatitis B, weight loss and jaundice is hepatocellular carcinoma. Metastases, hemangioma and FNH do not raise AFP, and cholangiocarcinoma is less associated with AFP.
HBV can cause HCC even without cirrhosis; AFP > 400 ng/mL supports HCC.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man with a history of chronic hepatitis B infection presents with right upper quadrant abdominal pain and unintentional weight loss. Examination reveals a firm, irregular mass in the right liver lobe. Laboratory tests show elevated alpha-fetoprotein (AFP). Ultrasound of the abdomen reveals a hypervascular liver mass. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
e:
A firm irregular mass, raised AFP and a hypervascular lesion on ultrasound in chronic hepatitis B = hepatocellular carcinoma. Metastases are usually multiple and hypovascular, haemangioma and FNH do not raise AFP, and an abscess is fever with a cystic lesion.
HCC is hypervascular in the arterial phase with washout later.

questions.q: A 65-year-old male with a history of chronic hepatitis B infection and cirrhosis presents to the outpatient clinic for a routine follow-up. He reports feeling well but has noticed some intermittent abdominal pain and a new onset of fatigue over the past few months. Alpha- fetoprotein (AFP) level: 350 ng/mL. An abdominal ultrasound shows a 4 cm lesion in the right lobe of the liver with irregular margins. What is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?
e:
A cirrhotic with chronic HBV, fatigue, abdominal pain, AFP 350 ng/mL and a 4 cm liver lesion with irregular margins has hepatocellular carcinoma. Adenoma, metastasis and FNH do not match the AFP and cirrhosis background.
New focal lesion in a cirrhotic liver: HCC until proven otherwise.

questions.q: A 65-year-old man with a history of cirrhosis due to hepatitis C presents for routine screening. An abdominal ultrasound reveals a 3 cm hypoechoic lesion in the liver with irregular borders. Serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) level is elevated. No other significant findings. What is the most likely diagnosis?
e:
A 3 cm hypoechoic lesion with irregular borders and raised AFP in a cirrhotic liver due to HCV = hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Metastasis, hemangioma, FNH and abscess are less probable.
Cirrhosis + raised AFP + focal lesion → triphasic CT/MRI.

questions.q: What is the preferred imaging technique for the initial diagnosis of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) in patients with cirrhosis?
e:
Ultrasound (with AFP) is the preferred initial imaging technique for HCC detection in cirrhotic patients, used for surveillance every 6 months; CT/MRI are used to characterise a lesion once found and X-ray is not used.
HCC surveillance: ultrasound ± AFP every 6 months.

questions.q: This is a focal hepatic lesion (arrow) on top of a cirrhotic liver. What is the best non-invasive method for diagnosing this focal lesion?
e:
The image shows a focal hepatic lesion (arrow) in a cirrhotic liver. The best non-invasive diagnostic test is triphasic CT (arterial enhancement with washout in the portal/delayed phase is diagnostic of HCC). Biopsy is invasive and AFP is not diagnostic alone.
Typical HCC on CT/MRI: arterial hyper-enhancement + washout; no biopsy needed.

questions.q: A patient presented with jaundice. Abdominal ultrasound shows a heterogeneous mass in the left lobe. What is the next step?
e:
The image shows a heterogeneous mass in the left lobe on ultrasound in a patient with jaundice; the next step is to characterise the mass with triphasic CT. Colonoscopy is irrelevant and MRI is a second-line option.
Characterise any focal liver lesion with dynamic (triphasic) CT or MRI.

questions.q: A 58-year-old man with a history of chronic hepatitis B infection presents with weight loss, abdominal discomfort and occasional jaundice. On examination, there is hepatomegaly and a palpable, firm mass in the right upper quadrant. Laboratory tests show elevated alpha- fetoprotein (AFP) levels. An abdominal ultrasound reveals a 3.5 cm hypervascular lesion in the right lobe of the liver. Further imaging with contrast-enhanced CT confirms a solitary lesion with arterial enhancement and washout in the portal venous phase. What is the most likely diagnosis, and what is the initial management step?
o: Hepatocellular carcinoma; consider surgical resection or locoregional therapy
Liver abscess; initiate antibiotics and drainage
Focal nodular hyperplasia; no treatment needed
e:
Chronic HBV, raised AFP and a solitary 3.5 cm hypervascular lesion with arterial enhancement and portal-venous washout on CT = hepatocellular carcinoma; initial management is resection or locoregional therapy (ablation/TACE). Metastasis, abscess, FNH and simple observation do not fit.
Early solitary HCC: resection, ablation or transplant.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman undergoes an abdominal ultrasound for vague right upper quadrant discomfort. The ultrasound reveals a well-circumscribed, hyperechoic lesion measuring about 3 cm in the right lobe of the liver. No other abnormalities are noted. She has no history of liver disease, alcohol intake or hepatitis. What is the most likely diagnosis of this focal lesion, and what is the typical histological feature?
o: Hepatocellular carcinoma; thickened hepatocyte plates and trabecular pattern
Liver abscess; necrotic debris with inflammatory infiltrate
Hemangioma; proliferation of blood vessels with a cavernous pattern
Focal nodular hyperplasia; central scar with malformed vessels
e:
The ultrasound image shows a well-circumscribed hyperechoic lesion (arrow) in the liver of a woman with no liver disease: a hemangioma, histologically proliferating vessels with a cavernous pattern. HCC occurs in cirrhosis, an abscess is febrile, and FNH has a central scar and is usually isodense.
Hemangioma: commonest benign liver tumour; hyperechoic, no biopsy needed.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man with a history of chronic HBV infection presents with weight loss, abdominal pain and jaundice. Physical examination reveals hepatomegaly and shifting dullness. Ultrasound shows a 4 cm mass in the liver with irregular borders. Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) levels are elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Liver metastasis from another primary tumor
e:
A 60-year-old with chronic HBV, weight loss, jaundice, shifting dullness, a 4 cm irregular liver mass and raised AFP has hepatocellular carcinoma. Metastasis, hemangioma and FNH do not raise AFP.
HBV → HCC; AFP and ultrasound are the screening tools.

questions.q: A patient presented with right hypochondrial pain referred to the right shoulder and dyspepsia to fatty meals. What could be the lesion seen on abdominal ultrasound as an echogenic focus in the gall bladder with a posterior (back) acoustic shadow?
e:
The ultrasound image shows an echogenic focus in the gallbladder with a posterior acoustic shadow: a gallbladder stone. RHC pain referred to the right shoulder with fatty meal dyspepsia fits biliary colic. Polyps are fixed without shadow and sludge (mud) does not shadow.
Stone = mobile echogenic focus + posterior shadow.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with a 2-day history of jaundice, right upper quadrant abdominal pain and dark urine. She reports nausea but no vomiting. On examination she has mild tenderness in the right upper abdomen and scleral icterus. Laboratory tests reveal elevated total bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase levels. An abdominal ultrasound was performed and showed this finding. What is the most likely diagnosis based on these ultrasound findings?
e:
Jaundice, dark urine and RUQ pain with raised bilirubin and ALP, and an ultrasound finding of an echogenic focus in the bile duct, indicate a common bile duct stone (choledocholithiasis). Acute cholecystitis, carcinoma of the gallbladder, HCC and pancreatic head tumour would not give this picture.
Dilated CBD + stone + jaundice → ERCP.

questions.q: A patient presented with jaundice. Abdominal ultrasound showed common bile duct stones. What is the next step?
e:
The ultrasound image (arrow) shows a common bile duct stone in a jaundiced patient; the next step is ERCP, which is both diagnostic and therapeutic (sphincterotomy and stone extraction). Stool analysis and colonoscopy are irrelevant.
ERCP = diagnose + treat bile duct stones; MRCP = non-invasive diagnosis only.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man presents with painless jaundice and recent unexplained weight loss. Laboratory tests reveal elevated bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase. Abdominal ultrasound shows dilated intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts, but no obvious mass is seen. The clinical suspicion is of a common bile duct stricture or small tumor not visualized on ultrasound. Which is the most appropriate next step to definitively diagnose and manage this patient?
o: Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) with brush cytology and possible stenting
e:
Painless jaundice with weight loss and dilated intra- and extra-hepatic ducts with no visible mass suggests a stricture or small tumour. ERCP with brush cytology and possible stenting gives a tissue diagnosis and relieves obstruction in the same session. MRCP and EUS-FNA are diagnostic only, and surgery is premature.
Painless jaundice + weight loss = pancreatic head cancer until proven otherwise (courvoisier: palpable non-tender gallbladder).
